findings.finding: Language — speech production (Northwestern Assessment of Verbs and Sentences, NAVS): Markedly impaired verb argument structure production (4th percentile). Sentence production requiring grammatical morphology: <2nd percentile. Sentence repetition: severely impaired — 3/22 on Northwestern Sentence Repetition Test (NSRT). Single-word comprehension (Peabody Picture Vocabulary Test, PPVT): 52nd percentile — PRESERVED. Object knowledge: 48th percentile — PRESERVED.

Speech motor (Apraxia of Speech Rating Scale, ASRS): Score 22/34 — consistent with mild-to-moderate acquired apraxia of speech. Features documented: consonant substitutions, additions, groping, inconsistent articulatory errors with increasing phrase complexity, islands of error-free speech on automatic sequences.

Verbal fluency: Letter fluency (F-words, 60 s): 3 words (severely impaired, <1st percentile). Category fluency (animals, 60 s): 14 words (48th percentile — PRESERVED). This severe dissociation between letter and category fluency is consistent with an anterior / production-based language impairment rather than semantic degradation.

Executive function (DKEFS Color-Word Interference — Inhibition): 18th percentile (low average). DKEFS Trails 4 (number-letter switching): 22nd percentile (low average). Executive dysfunction mild relative to profound language production deficit.
Episodic memory (HVLT-R): Immediate recall 9/12 trials 1-3 (40th percentile). Delayed recall 8/12 (35th percentile). Recognition 11/12 (52nd percentile). PRESERVED.

Behavioral measures (informant-rated): NPI-Q total score 4 — only 'aberrant motor behavior' subitem mildly positive (possibly stereotyped speech attempts). Frontal Behavioral Inventory (FBI): 9/72 — within normal limits for behavioral symptoms. No apathy, no disinhibition, no dietary change, no compulsive behaviors.

output.impression: Neuropsychological profile: severely impaired grammatical production and sentence-level repetition with mild-to-moderate apraxia of speech features. Single-word comprehension and object knowledge are preserved. A severe dissociation between letter fluency (impaired, production-dependent) and category fluency (preserved) indicates an anterior production-based impairment. Episodic memory, visuospatial function, and behavioral measures are intact. Pattern indicates a selective left inferior frontal/insular language-production deficit with sparing of posterior semantic systems

prohibited_recommendations: Do not attribute the progressive speech deficit to the prior TIA without new DWI evidence of ischemia — stroke-related aphasia stabilizes or improves; nfvPPA worsens.
Do not start acetylcholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine): no benefit established in nfvPPA and may worsen associated behavioral symptoms if they emerge.
Do not diagnose svPPA without testing single-word comprehension — the two PPA variants require opposite profiles and carry different implications for pathological substrate.
Do not order DaTscan in the absence of parkinsonism: no rigidity, bradykinesia, or supranuclear gaze palsy is present, and DaTscan does not distinguish nfvPPA from PSP-SPS.
required_recommendations: Apply Gorno-Tempini 2011 nfvPPA criteria: confirm at least one of agrammatism in production or effortful halting speech with apraxia of speech, AND preserved single-word comprehension and object knowledge.
Document the progressive nature of the deficit (18-month worsening trajectory) to distinguish nfvPPA from stroke recovery, which typically plateaus or improves.
Confirm that single-word comprehension is intact to distinguish nfvPPA from svPPA (svPPA = comprehension impaired) and from lvPPA (lvPPA = word retrieval deficit without AOS).
Monitor for emergence of vertical gaze palsy, falls, or axial rigidity that would suggest PSP-speech (SPS-PSP) overlap.
Refer for speech-language therapy and augmentative/alternative communication (AAC) planning to maintain communication function as the syndrome progresses.
Provide caregiver education and support resources specific to progressive aphasia.

avoided_actions.rationale: EEG is non-specific in nfvPPA and not part of the PPA diagnostic pathway unless seizures or rapidly progressive course raises concern for CJD or autoimmune encephalitis.
ECG has no role in the workup of progressive aphasia and is not indicated absent cardiac symptoms.
Echocardiography evaluates cardiac structure and is unrelated to a progressive neurodegenerative language syndrome.
Ambulatory cardiac monitoring is unrelated to the diagnostic question and not indicated without cardiac symptoms.
DaTscan is not indicated in nfvPPA without overt parkinsonism; no rigidity, bradykinesia, or supranuclear gaze palsy present.
MR spectroscopy has no established role in the routine nfvPPA diagnostic pathway.
Carotid duplex evaluates extracranial vascular disease and has no diagnostic role once a progressive neurodegenerative language syndrome is identified.

differential.diagnosis: Ischemic stroke / TIA (new lacunar event in speech areas)
differential.key_features: Prior TIA history and halting speech trigger vascular attribution; MRI DWI-negative and progressive 18-month course exclude acute ischemia.
Both are PPA subtypes, but svPPA presents with impaired single-word comprehension and anterior temporal atrophy — single-word comprehension is preserved here.

differential.diagnosis: Progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP) with speech predominant syndrome (SPS-PSP)
differential.key_features: PSP-SPS can present as nfvPPA with predominant AOS; absent vertical gaze palsy, falls, or axial rigidity makes SPS-PSP less likely at this stage.

differential.diagnosis: Corticobasal syndrome (CBS) with dominant language phenotype
differential.key_features: CBS can present with prominent aphasia and left hemisphere pathology; absent limb apraxia, alien-limb, or myoclonus on exam argues against.
lvPPA presents with word retrieval pauses and impaired sentence repetition but preserved grammar and no AOS; agrammatism and AOS distinguish nfvPPA.

key_clinical_evidence: The cardinal nfvPPA triad — agrammatic/telegraphic production with apraxia of speech, spared single-word comprehension, and spared episodic memory — is fully present; the diagnosis follows from applying Gorno-Tempini 2011 criteria.

Progressive worsening over 18 months, confirmed by the speech-language pathologist's referral note, is the decisive feature distinguishing nfvPPA from post-stroke aphasia, which does not worsen after the acute phase.
Left posterior frontal and insular atrophy on MRI, with a DWI-negative scan and no strategic infarct, rules out the red-herring vascular attribution.

The severe letter-fluency / preserved category-fluency dissociation is a production-based deficit signature, mechanistically opposite to svPPA (which shows category-fluency impairment from semantic degradation).

PSP with speech predominant syndrome (SPS-PSP) is a genuine mimic and remains on the differential; the absence of falls, supranuclear gaze palsy, and axial rigidity makes it less likely at this stage but warrants longitudinal monitoring.

results.finding: nfvPPA requires at least one of: agrammatism in language production, effortful halting speech with apraxia of speech (AOS). Supportive features include impaired comprehension of syntactically complex sentences but spared single-word comprehension and object knowledge. Imaging shows left posterior frontoinsular atrophy or hypometabolism. Pathology heterogeneous but FTLD-tau (CBD, PSP) most common; TDP-43 also reported.
results.title: Classification of primary progressive aphasia and its variants (Gorno-Tempini et al., Neurology 2011)

results.finding: FDG-PET characterises variant-specific metabolic patterns in PPA. nfvPPA shows left posterior frontal and insular hypometabolism. FDG-PET improves diagnostic accuracy over MRI alone when structural changes are subtle.
results.title: FDG-PET in FTD and PPA variants (Foster et al., Brain 2007)

results.finding: PPA variants are defined by the pattern of language deficit: nfvPPA (production/grammar), svPPA (single-word comprehension/semantics), lvPPA (word retrieval/sentence repetition). nfvPPA is most often associated with FTLD pathology. No disease-modifying therapy available. Speech-language therapy may maintain communication function.
results.title: Frontotemporal dementia — review (Bang et al., Lancet 2015)

nfvPPA_criteria_and_management.summary: Non-fluent/agrammatic primary progressive aphasia (nfvPPA) is classified by the Gorno-Tempini 2011 criteria and requires agrammatism in production or apraxia of speech as a core feature, with relative preservation of single-word comprehension. Left posterior frontal and insular atrophy and/or hypometabolism on FDG-PET are supportive imaging features. The syndrome is distinguished from svPPA (comprehension-predominant deficit) and lvPPA. Pathological substrate is heterogeneous (FTLD-tau subtypes predominate). No approved disease-modifying therapy. Speech-language therapy is the mainstay of supportive care. Clinical correlation recommended.

patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. C is a 69-year-old East Asian retired schoolteacher, widowed, referred to the neurology outpatient clinic by her speech-language pathologist after an 18-month course of progressive speech difficulty that initially failed to improve as expected following what the family physician had attributed to a 'speech stroke.' The patient has a history of a remote lacunar TIA four years ago from which she made a complete clinical recovery. Approximately 18 months ago, her adult daughter noticed that her mother — a lifelong Mandarin-English bilingual who had taught primary school for 35 years — was becoming increasingly effortful and telegraphic in conversation, producing shorter and shorter utterances with visible struggle and frequent sound errors. The family physician obtained a non-contrast head CT at that time, which was reported as normal, and attributed the speech changes to a possible new lacunar event that had been missed, maintaining her on aspirin. However, over the subsequent 18 months the speech difficulty has continued to worsen rather than plateau or improve — a trajectory inconsistent with a stroke-related deficit. The patient produces only 2-4 word telegraphic utterances with effortful, halting articulation. She omits grammatical function words and auxiliaries. She makes consonant substitution errors (apraxia of speech). In contrast, her comprehension of spoken language is fully preserved at the single-word and object level: she correctly follows all multi-step commands during the visit, identifies pictures accurately, and demonstrates intact object knowledge. She can communicate in writing more fluently than orally. There is no behavioral change, no apathy, no disinhibition, no perseverative behavior, no change in appetite or food preferences, no incontinence, and no falls. Episodic memory is described as intact by her daughter. She independently manages her household and finances. She has become isolated because communication is increasingly distressing. The speech-language pathologist who referred her explicitly noted: 'This is not a stroke recovery pattern — the progressive, worsening nonfluent agrammatic aphasia with apraxia of speech, in the absence of a new structural lesion, warrants neurological evaluation for a primary progressive language disorder.'

neurological_exam.additional: Daughter reports an 18-month history of progressive difficulty with speech. Initially attributed by the family physician to 'effects of a mini-stroke' given the prior TIA history. The patient herself is aware and distressed by her communication difficulty. She uses compensatory strategies such as writing notes and gesture. Episodic memory appears relatively intact by informant report: she independently manages finances, medication scheduling, and calendar. No behavioral disinhibition, no apathy, no repetitive behaviors, no dietary changes reported. No falls. No hallucinations. No urinary symptoms. No swallowing difficulty.
neurological_exam.coordination: Intact finger-nose, heel-shin bilaterally. Normal rapid alternating movements. No dysmetria.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Cranial nerves II-XII intact. No dysarthria of cerebellar type. No lower motor neuron bulbar signs. Palate elevates symmetrically. Gag intact. Tongue midline, no fasciculations. Jaw jerk absent. No facial asymmetry. Eye movements full, no supranuclear gaze palsy, no hypometric saccades.
neurological_exam.gait: Normal cadence and stride length. Normal arm swing bilaterally. No parkinsonian features. Tandem gait intact. Romberg negative.
neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and cooperative. Anxious about speaking. Spontaneous speech markedly reduced in fluency and phrase length: produces 2-4 word telegraphic utterances with visible articulatory effort, frequent hesitations, and intermittent consonant substitutions (e.g., 'spook' for 'spoke'). Agrammatic constructions evident — omits auxiliary verbs and grammatical function words when attempting longer phrases. Single-word comprehension tested with picture-pointing: intact (correctly identifies all 15 pictured objects on command). Object knowledge: intact (correctly identifies function of all 10 objects presented). Repetition: marked difficulty with multi-word phrases (repeats 'no ifs, ands, or buts' as 'no ifs an buts'). Reading aloud: slow and effortful but largely accurate for single words. Writing: somewhat telegraphic but better preserved than oral production. MoCA 24/30: loses 3 points on language subscores (verbal fluency F-words: 3 in 60 seconds, markedly impaired; naming 2/3), 2 on executive tasks (trails 0/1, cube copy 1/1), 1 on memory (4/5 delayed recall). Digit span forward 6, backward 4 — preserved.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone bilaterally. Strength 5/5 throughout all muscle groups. No tremor, no rigidity, no bradykinesia. No alien-limb phenomenon. No limb apraxia on examination when verbal instructions are bypassed (patient can imitate pantomimed actions accurately).
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ symmetric throughout upper and lower extremities. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No Hoffman sign. No primitive reflexes (palmomental, grasp, snout absent).
neurological_exam.sensory: Normal to light touch, pinprick, and proprioception bilaterally. No cortical sensory loss.
